title: Daubenton's perennial kale
subtitle: A sterile, perennial kale propagated by cuttings and harvested year-round.
excerpt: Daubenton's kale is a perennial kale that does not set seed. It is propagated from cuttings and produces leaves almost year-round in temperate UK conditions, with the heaviest harvest in late winter and spring when little else is available.
sourceNotes: Plant characteristics from Agroforestry Research Trust species data (agroforestry.co.uk). Growing method from Garden Organic perennial vegetables guidance. UK hardiness and performance data from current growing experience.

glossaryTerms.definition: A plant variety that produces no viable seed. Sterile cultivars do not spread or self-sow. They are propagated by vegetative means: cuttings, division, or layering. Daubenton's kale and Bocking 14 comfrey are sterile cultivars used in UK permaculture.

content.text: of perennial kale. It does not set seed and is propagated from stem cuttings. In a temperate UK garden, it produces leaves through most of the year including winter, with the most productive harvest in late winter and spring when annual kale and other brassicas are not yet in season.

Daubenton's kale is not available as seed. Buy rooted cuttings from specialist perennial vegetable suppliers in spring, or take cuttings from an established plant. Push 10 cm stem cuttings into a pot of compost in spring or early autumn. They root within three to four weeks.

Daubenton's kale does well in full sun to partial shade. It is hardy to approximately H5 (down to minus 10 to minus 15 degrees Celsius) but may lose leaves in a hard winter. In colder gardens or exposed sites, plant against a south-facing wall for extra warmth.

Plant out rooted cuttings in March to April or September into a prepared bed. Space plants 60 to 90 cm apart. Water in well. The plant grows slowly in the first season and speeds up from the second year onwards. In its first winter it may look sparse; from the second winter it is more productive.

Harvest young leaves and stem tips throughout the year. The flavour is milder than curly kale and the leaf texture is softer. Use raw in salads, lightly steamed, or in soups. Cut young stem tips 15 cm back to encourage bushy growth rather than a tall, leggy plant.

Cut the plant back hard to 20 to 30 cm above the ground each spring. This prevents it becoming woody and promotes a flush of new growth. Take cuttings from the pruned stems to propagate new plants. A well-managed plant in good soil lasts four to five years before it needs replacing.

items.symptom: Plant became tall and leggy with few leaves
items.cause: Not cut back in spring, or grown in too much shade.
items.fix: Cut hard to 20-30 cm in early spring. Move to a sunnier spot if shade is the cause.

items.cause: Cabbage white butterfly larvae. Perennial kale gets the same pest pressure as annual brassicas.
items.fix: Check leaves regularly from July onwards. Hand-pick caterpillars. Cover with fine mesh netting in areas with high butterfly pressure.

items.cause: Hard frost in an exposed site without adequate drainage.
items.fix: Replace with a new cutting taken before winter. In exposed gardens, plant against a south-facing wall or cover with fleece in periods below minus 10 degrees Celsius.
